prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active peptide form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, but unanimity of opening rank is not the argument. The argument is that this is a discernible change in a field produced by a specific, traceable discovery chain: the incretin effect and GLP-1 secretion physiology (Holst), the biology of GLP-1 action and its receptor (Drucker), and identification of the active truncated peptide GLP-1(7-36)amide (Mojsov) as the form that made therapeutic design rational. That chain has been confirmed by large independent randomized trials and by wide clinical use, and its effects now extend beyond glycaemia to weight, cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The impact has become apparent after decades, which is the kind of maturity that matters for a prize recognising a discovery rather than a career. A single-achievement prize with a physiology-centred credit fits this better than adding a second part, because no other shortlisted candidate matches its combination of mechanism and consequence, and splitting the prize would dilute the strongest case.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Four credited people cannot fit into three seats, and the peptide-characterisation story is contested; Habener's group, which is not on the supplied credit list, may have a claim comparable to Mojsov's, and Knudsen's industrial development of liraglutide and semaglutide is arguably what actually reached patients. A prize that favours physiology over drug development, or the reverse, will be criticised by one side. There is also a risk that the committee is carried by the clinical and public prominence of semaglutide and tirzepatide, which is not the same as scientific originality.

responses.point: The chair proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating Knudsen's pharmacological engineering of long-acting analogues as the third pillar and regarding Mojsov's weighting as disputed.
responses.response: I take the objection seriously, but I would still credit Mojsov over Knudsen. The prize recognises a discovery. Knudsen's contribution is excellent drug design built on the peptide and receptor biology already established, whereas Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form and its insulinotropic activity is part of what the discovery rests on. Choosing Knudsen would move the prize toward drug development, and I think that would be a departure from how we usually draw the line. I accept that priority around Mojsov is disputed and that I am relying on recalled history. If the committee found that her claim cannot be verified from the record, I would reopen the third seat.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked CAR-T cells second, citing durable remissions in refractory B-cell malignancies, multiple approved products and years of follow-up, and treated missing earlier chimeric-receptor credit as a limitation rather than a disqualifier.
responses.response: I agree CAR-T is a real new modality, but I rank it below cGAS-STING and orexin. The principal obstacle for me is that the concept of the chimeric receptor (Eshhar, Kuwana and others) sits outside the supplied names, so the three-person set of June, Sadelain and Rosenberg describes costimulation, clinical translation and adoptive transfer, which are distinct strands, rather than one discovery. Efficacy is also still confined to haematological cancers, with open questions on toxicity and durability. I would not oppose it in a later year once attribution is cleaner, but I would not choose it as this year's configuration.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius proposed Hall alone for TOR, arguing that Schreiber's FKBP12-rapamycin work and Sabatini's mTOR work are more incremental or complicating and that a single laureate is the cleanest configuration.
responses.response: I agree Hall is the anchor and that the TOR credit is complicated, but I would not call Schreiber incremental, because the identification of the rapamycin-FKBP12 target is part of how TOR was recognised as a conserved kinase pathway. Where I disagree is on the practical consequence. A Hall-only prize is a fair reading if the committee is willing to leave out much of the mammalian chain, but then we should say so openly and not pretend it is a clean story. I would keep TOR as a strong candidate for a later year with a defensible two-person or one-person design, and I do not think it displaces GLP-1 now.

responses.point: El-Manira ranked optogenetics second as a method with exceptional originality and breadth that reshaped circuit neuroscience, with first clinical use in vision restoration, while acknowledging that three seats force painful exclusions among six credited people.
responses.response: The scientific impact is not in doubt, but I place it below mechanisms with disease consequences. My concern is twofold. First, the credit cannot be resolved into three names without excluding Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck, and a prize that creates a visible injustice is a weaker prize. Second, this is a tool, and I think a discovery with a human disease mechanism, such as orexin in narcolepsy or cGAS-STING in innate immunity, fits the criterion of a discovery with discernible change in medicine more directly. I could support it if we find the credit question has a principled answer, but I have not yet seen one.

uncertainties: Whether the third seat should go to Mojsov or Knudsen, and whether Habener's group should enter the discussion despite not being on the supplied credit list.
Whether a prize for GLP-1 should be framed as physiology or as translation to therapy, which affects the citation wording and the weight given to industrial development.

If GLP-1 were for some reason set aside, I have not settled whether cGAS-STING (mechanism-heavy, clean two names, therapy pending) or orexin (disease link, but a priority conflict between orexin and hypocretin groups) is the better second choice.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the shortlisted candidates is apparent from my profile. My work with Ronald Evans on nuclear receptors and my collaboration with Johan Ericson are not connected to any shortlisted ballot. I have co-authored with Per Svenningsson (and once with Abdel El Manira), but this is not a connection to any candidate and I do not regard it as requiring recusal.
